- When sentiment is consistently high (≥0.67) over recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast slope or cap upward momentum.
- When sentiment is consistently low (≤0.33), model underestimates; adjust upward slightly, especially if price is trending down.
- After sharp price spikes (e.g., +10%+ in 3–5 days), model often overshoots and fails to correct — apply a “cool-down” rule: reduce forecast by 5–10% for next 3–5 periods.
- If true outcome shows strong mean reversion (e.g., 3–5 consecutive days of price decline after peak), model often fails to recognize — add a “reversion buffer” to forecast, especially if sentiment is mixed or neutral.
- For 30-day forecasts, model often fails to capture short-term sentiment-driven volatility — if sentiment swings sharply, adjust forecast to reflect sentiment volatility (e.g., ±3–5% band around mean).
- If sentiment history shows alternating high/low (e.g., 0.67, 0.33, 0.67), model tends to overfit recent sentiment — use sentiment smoothing (e.g., 3-period average) to avoid overreaction.
- When true outcome deviates from forecast by >10% in first 5 days, model often fails to adjust — apply “early correction” rule: adjust forecast by -10% to -20% for next 3–5 periods if sentiment is neutral or declining.
